title: Debates sought on the BBC and autism strategy
label: 17 November 2026 · Backbench debate requests
summary: The committee heard requests for debates on the BBC’s future and the Government’s next national autism strategy. Grahame Morris wanted MPs to discuss BBC cuts and funding before Christmas, preferably in the Commons Chamber. Alison Hume wanted a Westminster Hall debate while the autism strategy was still being developed. The committee gave no public decision on either request.

glossary.definition: A document setting out the Government’s policy proposals.
The document setting out how the BBC is governed and what it is expected to do.
The BBC service that provides news and other programmes to audiences around the world.
The main debating room of the House of Commons.
A separate venue where MPs can hold debates outside the main Commons Chamber.
The Commons committee that examines the work of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.
A UK law requiring the Government to produce and update a national autism strategy.
Special educational needs and disabilities; the term used for support for children and young people with these needs.

chapters.title: The BBC’s future
chapters.takeaway: Grahame Morris wanted MPs to discuss BBC cuts and the next charter before Christmas, with a Commons debate his first choice.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Let’s start with Grahame Morris’s request for a debate.

evidence.quote: We will first consider the application from Grahame Morris.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: I’m asking for a 90-minute debate on the BBC before Christmas. We expect the Government’s long-awaited White Paper by then, and the BBC is already making decisions about jobs and programmes that will shape the service under its next charter.

evidence.quote: I am asking for time before Christmas because we are expecting the Government’s long-awaited White Paper later this year, before Christmas.
The BBC is already making decisions about jobs and programmes.
which will shape the service that is shaped by the new charter.
to debate this in a 90-minute debate.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: MPs should be able to put their constituents’ views on record and ask Ministers what they plan to do. In my area, BBC Radio Newcastle and “Look North” show why local radio and regional news matter, especially to older people and those who can’t easily leave home.

evidence.quote: We feel that Back-Bench MPs should have the opportunity to put their constituents’ views on the record and ask Ministers how they propose to respond.
In my own constituency, Easington in the north-east, BBC Radio Newcastle and “Look North” are practical examples of what our public service broadcasting means for constituents.
especially to people who rely on broadcast services, particularly the elderly and housebound.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: The broadcasting unions supporting the parliamentary group I’m involved in want urgent action on cuts, reliable funding for the BBC, separate and secure funding for the World Service, and a formal say for workers on the BBC’s board without compromising its editorial independence.

evidence.quote: The five unions supporting the broadcasting, entertainment and arts unions all-party parliamentary group, of which I am an officer, represent people who report, write, perform, record and produce BBC output.

Those trade unions want urgent action on cuts, a sustainable public service, a funding settlement, secure and separate funding for the World Service, and a formal voice for workers on an editorially independent BBC board.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: Cuts to staff and programme-making affect what audiences can watch and listen to, as well as jobs and freelance work across the UK. A debate would let MPs question the Government’s choices before the next charter takes effect.

evidence.quote: Cuts to staff and commissioning affect the quality and range of programmes that audiences can expect, as well as threatening jobs and freelance work across the UK.
A debate would allow Members to test the Government’s approach to those choices and ask what can be done before the next charter takes effect.

turns.speaker: Will Stone
turns.text: A debate in the Commons Chamber needs at least 15 MPs’ names. Could you find four more supporters, or would you accept a debate in Westminster Hall?

evidence.quote: For a Chamber debate, we need a minimum of 15 Member names. Would you be happy to go away and get four additional names, or would you be content with a Westminster Hall debate?

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: I’m fairly confident I can find more names. MPs from across parties have told me they’re interested. The Chamber is my first choice, but the most important thing is to hold the debate before Christmas. If there’s no Chamber time, I’d accept 90 minutes in Westminster Hall.

evidence.quote: I have spoken to several Members, from across parties, who are interested and have indicated that they would welcome the opportunity to speak in such a debate.

The short answer is yes, I am fairly confident that we could get more names, but if you cannot spare the time in the Chamber before Christmas, we would take a 90-minute debate in Westminster Hall. But our first choice would be the Chamber, if that is possible.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: I sit on the DCMS Committee, which examines culture and media policy. I’m concerned that “You and Yours”, the only live Radio 4 programme made outside London, is being axed. My constituents value it. I support this request and hope the debate can happen soon.

evidence.quote: I should advise Members that I sit on the DCMS Committee.
I am concerned about the fact that the only live programme made for BBC Radio 4 outside London, “You and Yours”, is being axed. I have many constituents who value that specialist consumer program.
I support your application and I hope that we can put it in, in a timely manner.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The committee staff will contact you. If the debate is on a Tuesday morning, it must be on a day when the relevant Government department is due to answer.

evidence.quote: The Clerks will be in touch with you, Grahame. If the debate is held on a Tuesday morning, you appreciate that it must be a morning when that Department is replying.

chapters.title: A new autism strategy
chapters.takeaway: Alison Hume sought a debate while the Government was preparing its next autism strategy, citing serious inequalities and limited progress so far.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Next is Alison Hume’s request for a debate.

evidence.quote: Our next applicant is Alison Hume. Over to you, Alison.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: I’m asking for a debate on what the Government’s next national autism strategy should prioritise. Autistic people still face severe inequalities: they die between six and 15 years earlier than the general population.

evidence.quote: my application for a Backbench Business debate on priorities for the Government's next national autism strategy.
autistic people continue to face some of the most extreme health inequalities in society.
autistic people die between 6 and 15 years earlier than the general population

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: Only 26% of autistic students say they feel happy at school, and only three in 10 autistic adults are in work—one of the lowest employment rates for any disability.

evidence.quote: Only 26% of autistic students say that they feel happy at school, and only three in 10 autistic adults are in work—that figure is among the lowest for any disability.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: The Autism Act 2009 requires the Government to produce and regularly update a strategy. But the House of Lords found that outcomes hadn’t improved despite those efforts. The current strategy expired at the end of June, and the Government says it will extend it while developing a replacement.

evidence.quote: The Autism Act 2009 required the Government to produce and regularly update a national autism strategy.
the House of Lords, which has done amazing work on this, found that, despite those efforts, outcomes have not improved.

The current strategy expired at the end of June 2026. The Government have said that they are committed to publishing a new strategy, and that the lifespan of the current strategy will be extended while a new one is developed.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: A debate now would let MPs from different parties contribute while the new strategy is being written. That matters as the Government introduces its new offer of support for children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities, known as SEND. I’m asking for Westminster Hall.

evidence.quote: a debate would be a timely opportunity for Members of Parliament from all parties to engage with the next autism strategy while it is being developed.
That is important, as the Government are rolling out the new SEND offer.
I would be very grateful if the Committee considered my application for a Westminster Hall debate.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: Those numbers are striking. Do you want the debate to coincide with a particular date, or would the next available slot work?

evidence.quote: Those are quite shocking numbers, so I can see the reason for requesting a debate. Is there a particular date you would like it to coincide with, or are you happy for it to be scheduled in the next available slot?

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: The next available slot would be fine.

evidence.quote: I would be very happy for it to be scheduled in the next available slot.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I assume the Department of Health would answer the debate?

evidence.quote: I presume the responding Department would be Health.
Yes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You’ve asked for a Thursday, so the restriction on Tuesday debates doesn’t apply. Committee staff will be in touch.

evidence.quote: Oh, you have asked for a Thursday anyway, so the Tuesday restriction does not apply—very good. As a member of the Committee, I think you know that the Clerks will be in touch.
